0.1-c1.q: Using the map: page 8.1 builds directly on one page. Which section is that page in?
options: Section 2, neural networks as functions
Section 4, how models are trained today
Section 6, mechanistic interpretability
0.1-c1.feedback: Page 8.1 builds directly on 4.3, optimizing a learned reward. On page 4.3 a model is trained against a reward model, which stands in for human judgment; page 8.1 studies optimizing any such proxy.

1.1-c1.q: LeCun’s 1989 zip-code reader and AlexNet (2012) were both convolutional networks trained with backpropagation. What did AlexNet have that the 1989 network did not?
options: A method for training the hidden layers
Far more training compute and over a million labeled images
The idea of applying one filter at every position
1.1-c1.feedback: Backpropagation and convolution were both in the 1989 network. What changed between 1989 and 2012 was computing power (GPUs) and data (ImageNet).

1.1-c2.q: Which statement fits the timeline best?
options: Deep learning took off when backpropagation was invented
Each AI winter ended when a new architecture was found
Most core methods were decades old when they started to work at scale
1.1-c2.feedback: Backpropagation (1970, 1986), convolutional networks (1989), and the LSTM (1997) waited until the 2010s, when compute and data caught up.

1.2-c1.q: Can a single perceptron compute “\(x_1\) and not \(x_2\)”, which outputs 1 only for the input (1, 0)?
options: Yes
No
1.2-c1.feedback: Yes. Its only 1-point, (1, 0), sits at a corner of the square, and a line can cut that corner off from the other three points. For example, weights 1 and \(-1\) with bias \(-0.5\).

1.2-c2.q: Which statement fits the record best?
options: Minsky and Papert proved that networks with hidden layers cannot compute XOR, and this ended the funding
Minsky and Papert proved real limits of perceptrons, and AI funding also fell for other reasons
The perceptron convergence theorem was shown to be false
1.2-c2.feedback: The book’s theorems are correct. They concern perceptrons, and they do not show that every network with a hidden layer is limited in the same way. The fall in funding had several documented causes, including the Lighthill report and the Mansfield Amendment.

1.3-c1.q: Suppose an activation function’s derivative is never larger than 0.5, and each layer’s weights multiply the signal by about 1. In a network with 12 layers, at most how large can the gradient at layer 1 be, compared with the gradient at layer 12?
options: About 1/12 as large
About 1/2,000 as large
The same size
1.3-c1.feedback: Backpropagation multiplies the gradient by one factor of at most 0.5 for each of the 11 layers between layer 12 and layer 1, and \(0.5^{11} = 1/2{,}048\). The shrinkage is geometric in depth, not proportional to it.

1.4-c1.q: Which of these did LeCun’s 1989 zip-code network already have?
options: Training on GPUs
A convolutional architecture trained with backpropagation
More than a million labeled training images
1.4-c1.feedback: LeCun’s network was convolutional and trained with backpropagation in 1989. AlexNet added a far larger labeled dataset, training on GPUs, ReLU, and dropout.

1.4-c2.q: A layer that connected every pixel of a 240 by 160 image to every position of a 240 by 160 output would need about 1.5 billion parameters. A convolutional layer with one 3 by 3 filter needs 9. Why so few?
options: The same filter is reused at every position
It looks at only some of the pixels
It uses the ReLU activation function
1.4-c2.feedback: Every position uses the same nine numbers, and each output depends only on the nearby pixels. A detector for an edge is useful anywhere in the image, so one copy of it serves every position.

1.5-c1.q: Training compute is roughly proportional to parameters times training tokens, and Chinchilla says both should grow in equal proportion. With 4 times the compute, how should each change?
options: 4 times the parameters, same tokens
About 2 times each
Same parameters, 4 times the tokens
1.5-c1.feedback: If parameters and tokens each grow by a factor \(k\), compute grows by \(k^2\). For \(k^2 = 4\), \(k = 2\).

1.5-c2.q: Kaplan et al. found that loss falls as a power law in compute: \(L = (C_0 / C)^{\alpha}\) for constants \(C_0\) and \(\alpha\). Plotted with log loss against log compute, what does this look like?
options: A straight line sloping down
A curve that flattens to a floor
A sudden drop at one compute level
1.5-c2.feedback: Taking logs gives \(\log L = \alpha \log C_0 - \alpha \log C\), a straight line with slope \(-\alpha\). The same reasoning explains the straight trend line in the compute chart: exponential growth is a straight line on a log axis.

1.6-c1.q: Does fine-tuning with human feedback mainly add knowledge to a model?
options: Yes, the feedback teaches it new facts
No, it mainly changes which behaviors the model produces
No, it leaves the model’s behavior unchanged
1.6-c1.feedback: The evidence points to the second answer. Most knowledge comes from pretraining (Zhou et al. 2023), and the post-trained model in the tool repeats its base model’s gaps, such as the Einstein and Mars errors, while answering in a different form.

1.6-c2.q: The chat and reasoning columns use the same parameters. Why did the reasoning model count the letters correctly when the chat model did not?
options: Thinking mode loads a larger network
The reasoning model was trained on this exact question
It wrote out the letters first, so it spent more passes through the network and could read its own intermediate results
1.6-c2.feedback: Each written token is another pass through the same network, and each pass can read everything written so far. Spelling the word one letter at a time turned a hard single step into many easy ones.

2.2-c1.q: A sigmoid neuron has \(w = (1, 2)\) and \(b = -1\). You change it to \(w = (2, 4)\) and \(b = -2\). What happens?
options: The line moves halfway toward the origin
The line stays where it is, and the output changes faster across it
The line turns
2.2-c1.feedback: The new sum is twice the old one, so it is zero at the same inputs: the line stays put. Away from the line the sum is twice as large, so the sigmoid goes from near 0 to near 1 over half the distance.

2.3-c1.q: A network has 50 layers, each of width 1,000, and no activation functions. Which functions of its input can it compute?
options: Any continuous function, given enough training
Piecewise linear functions with many pieces
Only linear functions, the same as one layer
2.3-c1.feedback: Each layer is linear, and a composition of linear maps is a linear map, so the 50 layers multiply out to one matrix and one bias vector. Depth adds nothing without activation functions.

2.3-c2.q: In the playground, a network with ReLU in layer 1 and no activation function in layers 2 and 3 classified the spirals well. Which network computes the same family of functions?
options: One linear layer
One hidden ReLU layer of width 8 followed by the output neuron
Three hidden ReLU layers
2.3-c2.feedback: Layers 2 and 3 and the output neuron multiply out to one linear map, so what remains is one ReLU layer followed by one linear output: a network with one hidden layer.

2.4-c2.q: A trained network’s boundary in the input plane is curved. Where does the curvature come from?
options: The output neuron draws a curved boundary
The hidden layers move the points; the output’s straight boundary, traced back to the input, is curved
The training data contains the curve
2.4-c2.feedback: The output is one neuron, so its boundary is flat in the space it sees. That space is the input after the hidden layers have bent it, so the same boundary looks curved in the input.

2.5-c1b.q: Suppose a model were trained with the linear rule instead of the log rule. Would you expect the probabilities it reports to be calibrated?
options: Yes, any scoring rule leads to calibration
No, training would push its reports toward 0 and 1
No, training would push its reports toward one half
2.5-c1b.feedback: The linear rule is not proper: its expected loss is lowest at an end, so a model trained with it gains by reporting 0 or 1. The push toward calibration comes from the rule being strictly proper.

2.5-c2.q: What kind of learning is pretraining?
options: Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning, with targets taken from the text
Clustering without targets
2.5-c2.feedback: Each next token in the training text is the target, and the model is scored on it with the log rule. No reward signal is involved.

2.6-c1.q: A loss surface is a valley with curvature 400 across it and 1 along it. With plain gradient descent, which learning rate is the largest of these that converges?
2.6-c1.feedback: Convergence needs \(\eta\) below 2 divided by the largest curvature, here \(2/400 = 0.005\). Of the three, only 0.004 qualifies. At that rate the direction along the valley, with curvature 1, shrinks by a factor of only 0.996 per step, so it takes many steps.

2.6-c2.q: On the two-minimum surface, the same start and the same learning rate end in different minima depending on the noise. What does this show about training?
options: Training always finds the lowest loss
The data and loss do not fix which parameters training finds
Noise only changes how fast training ends
2.6-c2.feedback: The loss surface was the same in every run; only the noise differed, and the runs ended in different minima. In large networks the same holds: runs that differ only in such details as the random seed or the order of the examples can do equally well on held-out test data and still behave differently on new kinds of inputs.D’Amour et al. (2022), “Underspecification Presents Challenges for Credibility in Modern Machine Learning,” Journal of Machine Learning Research 23. So what a trained network does is not chosen by anyone directly; it has to be found out afterward, which is the work of sections 6 and 8 (page 5.5 returns to this).

2.7-c1.q: A network has one loss and a million parameters. Forward-mode differentiation gives, in one pass, the derivatives of every node with respect to one chosen parameter. About how many passes does each method need for the full gradient?
options: One each
A million each
Forward mode a million, backpropagation one
2.7-c1.feedback: Forward mode follows one parameter per pass, so it needs a million passes. Backpropagation starts from the single loss and reaches every parameter in one backward pass, after one forward pass.

2.7-c2.q: In a graph, a value \(v\) feeds two operations. The derivatives they send back to \(v\) are 0.3 and \(-0.5\). What is \(\partial L/\partial v\)?
options: 0.3, the first one to arrive
2.7-c2.feedback: Where paths meet, the contributions add: \(0.3 + (-0.5) = -0.2\). This is the multivariable chain rule: the loss depends on \(v\) through both operations.

2.8-c1.q: A model’s training error is zero. What do you know about its test error?
options: It is also zero
It must be large, because the model has overfit
Nothing yet; it has to be measured on held-out data
2.8-c1.feedback: Zero training error is consistent with any test error. In the playground, degrees 11 and 30 both have zero training error, and for the first set of points their test errors are about 300,000 and 1.0. Only held-out data tells them apart.

2.8-c2.q: With 40 points, where would you expect the test error of these polynomial fits to peak?
options: Near degree 11, as before
Near degree 39
At degree 3
2.8-c2.feedback: The peak sits where the number of coefficients, the degree plus one, equals the number of points: degree 39 for 40 points.

3.1-c1.q: GPT-2 receives “·strawberry” as the single token 41236. What does its input tell it directly about the letters in that word?
options: The letters and their order
Nothing about the letters
Only how many letters there are
3.1-c1.feedback: The input is the id 41236 and nothing else; anything the model knows about the letters of that token it learned from its training text. This is why a model can find it hard to reverse or count the letters of a word: those letters are not in what it reads.

3.1-c2.q: GPT-2 reads at most 1,024 tokens at once. Judging from the English and Persian examples, how much Persian text fits in that window, compared with English text of the same meaning?
options: About the same amount
About one sixth as much
About six times as much
3.1-c2.feedback: The same sentence took 5 tokens in English and 29 in Persian, so the window holds about 5/29, roughly one sixth, as much Persian content.

3.2-c1.q: Take GPT-2 small before training, with its parameters at their random starting values. What would the nearest neighbors of the token “·bank” be?
options: Words about money, as after training
Unrelated tokens, close by chance
The tokens with ids next to its id
3.2-c1.feedback: The embeddings are parameters, set to random numbers before training. Only training on text moves the vectors of tokens that occur in similar contexts close together, so before training the nearest neighbors are whatever tokens happen to be close at random.

3.2-c2.q: Word2vec reads the sentence “we sat on the bank of the river.” Which vector does it use for bank?
options: The same vector as in “the bank raised its rates”
A vector close to river and water
A new vector, computed from the sentence
3.2-c2.feedback: Word2vec has one vector per word, whatever the sentence. The first layer of a transformer works the same way: the embedding of a token is one row of a matrix. Only the later layers make the vector at each position depend on the context.

3.3-c1.q: As the temperature approaches 0, what does sampling become?
options: Always taking the most likely token
Drawing every token with equal probability
Drawing from the model’s own probabilities
3.3-c1.feedback: Dividing by a small \(T\) makes the gap between the largest logit and every other logit huge, so softmax puts almost all the probability on the most likely token. In the limit this is greedy decoding. As \(T\) grows large, the distribution approaches equal probabilities instead.

3.3-c2.q: Two tokens have logits 2 and 1, and no other token is possible. At \(T = 0.5\), about what probability does the first token get?
3.3-c2.feedback: Dividing by 0.5 gives 4 and 2, so the probability is \(e^4 / (e^4 + e^2) = 1 / (1 + e^{-2}) \approx 0.88\). At \(T = 1\) it would be \(1 / (1 + e^{-1}) \approx 0.73\).

3.3-c3.q: You give a chat model sampling at \(T = 1\) the same question twice and get two different answers. What does this show?
options: The model changed between the two questions
Each answer is one draw from the same distribution
At least one of the answers is an error
3.3-c3.feedback: The model and its distribution are the same both times; sampling drew different tokens. To learn what the model tends to say, look at many draws or at the probabilities themselves.

3.4-c1.q: In a model with the causal mask, every position has the same key. What does position 3 receive?
options: Its own value, \(v_3\)
3.4-c1.feedback: Equal keys give equal scores for any query, so softmax gives equal weights to all the positions position 3 may see: 1/3 each to positions 1, 2, and 3. Position 4 is masked.

3.4-c2.q: With the causal mask on, which change can make token 2’s output depend on token 3?
options: Point \(q_2\) along \(k_3\)
Make \(k_3\) very long
None of these
3.4-c2.feedback: The mask gives token 3 a weight of exactly 0 for token 2, whatever the scores, so nothing about token 3 reaches token 2 in this layer.

3.4-c3.q: Compute this one by hand. Queries and keys have \(d_k = 4\) entries. Position 2 has query \(q_2 = (1.1, 1.1, 0, 0)\); the keys are \(k_1 = (0, 0, 1, 1)\) and \(k_2 = (1, 1, 0, 0)\); the values are \(v_1 = (4, 0)\) and \(v_2 = (0, 4)\). Use \(e^{1.1} \approx 3\). What does position 2 receive?
3.4-c3.feedback: The dot products are 0 and 2.2; divided by \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), the scores are 0 and 1.1. Softmax gives weights \(1/(1+3) = 1/4\) and \(3/4\). The output is \(\tfrac14 (4, 0) + \tfrac34 (0, 4) = (1, 3)\).

3.5-c1.q: A text contains “Hermione Granger” once. Much later it reaches “Hermione” again. At that position, what does an induction head attend to, and which next token does it make more likely?
options: The first “Hermione”; it makes “Hermione” more likely
The first “Granger”; it makes “Granger” more likely
The token just before the current one; it makes that token more likely
3.5-c1.feedback: The current token is A = “Hermione”. Earlier, A was followed by B = “Granger”, so the induction head attends to that “Granger” and copies it toward the prediction.

3.5-c2.q: On random tokens repeated twice, which token of the second copy does the model still predict badly?
options: The first token of the second copy
The last token of the second copy
None of them
3.5-c2.feedback: The first token of the second copy is predicted at the last token of the first copy, which has appeared only once, so there is no earlier copy to match and nothing to copy. From the second token on, the current token has appeared before, and the induction heads can copy what came after it. Over 100 random sequences the loss on the first token of the second copy averages 11.1, against 0.53 for the rest of the second copy.

3.6-c1.q: Can layer 8 use information computed by layer 2?
options: Yes
No; each layer sees only the output of the layer before it
Only if layer 2’s result passes through every layer in between unchanged
3.6-c1.feedback: Layer 2’s output was added to the residual stream, and layer 8 reads the residual stream, which still contains that addition. Later layers add to it but do not replace it, so nothing has to pass layer 2’s result along. They can, though, add something that cancels part of it.

3.6-c2.q: In the Japan prompt, layer 9’s attention part raises “Tokyo” at the last position from 0.07 to 0.76. What can the attention part do there that the MLP part cannot?
options: Apply an activation function
Bring information from the residual streams at other positions, such as “Japan”
Change the residual streams at earlier positions
3.6-c2.feedback: The MLP acts on each position separately, so at the last position it can use only what is already in that position’s residual stream. Attention takes a weighted average of values computed from the residual streams at the positions it may see, itself and earlier ones. Neither part changes the earlier positions: in a language model, information moves only forward.

3.7-c1.q: Which of these steps can make one position’s vector depend on the tokens at other positions?
options: Normalize
The MLP
Attention
3.7-c1.feedback: Normalization and the MLP act on each position’s vector by itself; in the heat maps, each row of their output is computed from the same row of their input. Attention is the only step that combines positions, through the weighted average of values.

3.7-c2.q: Every entry of the residual stream entering a normalization step is doubled. Ignoring the tiny constant added to the variance, what happens to the output of that step?
options: It doubles
It stays the same
It is multiplied by four
3.7-c2.feedback: Doubling a vector doubles its mean and its standard deviation, so subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation gives the same result. A linear map would double its output, so normalization is not linear. (A tiny constant added to the variance before dividing makes the output change very slightly.)

3.7-c3.q: Which steps of the forward pass are not linear functions of their input?
options: Only the softmax at the end
Normalization, attention, the activation function, and the final softmax
Every step that has parameters
3.7-c3.feedback: Normalization divides by a quantity computed from its input; attention applies softmax and multiplies two quantities that both depend on the input; the activation function and the final softmax are nonlinear functions. The matrix multiplications with parameters, the bias additions, and the additions to the residual stream are linear or affine.

3.8-c1.q: A lab has 100 times Chinchilla’s compute (70 billion parameters, 1.4 trillion tokens) and follows the rule of about 20 tokens per parameter, with \(C \approx 6ND\). Which model should it train?
options: 700 billion parameters on 14 trillion tokens
7 trillion parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens
70 billion parameters on 140 trillion tokens
3.8-c1.feedback: With \(D = 20N\), compute is \(C \approx 120N^2\), so 100 times the compute means \(\sqrt{100} = 10\) times the parameters and 10 times the tokens.

3.8-c2.q: A scaling law predicts that a new model ten times larger will have a lower loss. What does that tell you about whether it will be able to do three-digit multiplication?
options: It will, because lower loss improves every task
Nothing directly about that one task
It will not, because loss and abilities are unrelated
3.8-c2.feedback: The law predicts the next-token loss averaged over all the test text, and one task is a small part of that average. A lower average is compatible with large gains on some tasks and none on others.

4.1-c1.q: Which stage gives the model most of its knowledge of the world?
options: Pretraining
Supervised fine-tuning
Learning from feedback
Reinforcement learning on checkable tasks
4.1-c1.feedback: Pretraining. In the tool, the base model already knew all 24 facts, and later stages left that knowledge about where it was while changing behavior a great deal. Pretraining also uses most of the training data and compute.

4.1-c2.q: A lab trains a model by writing a reference answer for each of 100,000 prompts and fine-tuning on them with the cross-entropy loss. Which kind of learning is this?
options: Reinforcement learning, because the answers express human preferences
Supervised learning, because the targets are fixed text
Neither, because no reward model is used
4.1-c2.feedback: This is supervised fine-tuning, stage 2. The model is not scored on its own outputs; it is trained to predict tokens of text written in advance. Reinforcement learning begins when the model’s own outputs are scored.

4.2-c1.q: Suppose 10 is added to the score of every response. What happens to the reward model’s predicted preferences?
options: Nothing changes
Every preference becomes closer to certain
Every preference moves toward 0.5
4.2-c1.feedback: The prediction depends only on \(r(A) - r(B)\), which adding the same number to both leaves unchanged. Scores are therefore defined only up to a constant, and a reward model’s absolute scores mean nothing by themselves.

4.3-c1.q: Two responses get the same reward model score. The starting model gives one of them probability 0.2 and the other 0.1. Under \(\pi^{*}\), how do their probabilities compare as \(\beta\) changes?
options: They become equal once \(\beta\) is small
The rarer one catches up as \(\beta\) grows
The first is always twice as likely as the second
4.3-c1.feedback: Both are multiplied by the same factor \(\exp(r/\beta)\) before normalizing, so the ratio of their probabilities stays at 0.2 to 0.1 for every \(\beta\). The reweighting changes probabilities only through differences in reward.

4.3-c2.q: A team lowers \(\beta\) step by step and sees the reward model’s average score rise every time. What does that show about true quality?
options: True quality is rising too
Nothing by itself; true quality may be rising or falling
True quality must be falling
4.3-c2.feedback: The reward model’s score rises as \(\beta\) falls whether or not quality does: in the tool it rose the whole way in both cases. Only an independent measure of quality, such as fresh human judgments, can show which case they are in.

4.4-c1.q: A small model fails to multiply two 20-digit numbers when it must write the answer at once, yet succeeds when it writes out partial products first. What is the best explanation?
options: Writing steps lets the model look up the answer in its training data
The written steps make the model larger
The task needs more steps in sequence than one pass provides; each written token adds a pass that can read the earlier results
4.4-c1.feedback: The network and its parameters are the same either way. Each written token is one more pass through the layers, and the text written so far carries intermediate results from one pass to the next, as the carries did in the addition models.

4.4-c2.q: A model’s forced answer is the same at every cut, from the empty chain of thought to the full one. What does this show?
options: The written reasoning did not determine this answer
The written reasoning is false
The model did not use its layers to compute the answer
4.4-c2.feedback: The answer was settled before the reasoning was written, so the reasoning cannot be what produced it. The reasoning may still be correct, and the model computed the answer in the passes that read the question.

5.1-c1.q: A one-hidden-layer ReLU network with 20 units has one input. At most how many straight pieces can its output have?
options: Any number, if the parameters are chosen well
5.1-c1.feedback: Each unit bends the output at one point, its kink, so 20 units give at most 20 bends and 21 pieces. A deeper network with 20 units can have many more.

5.1-c2.q: A network with a million hidden units is trained on a dataset and still fits it badly. Does this contradict the universal approximation theorem?
options: Yes: with that many units it should fit any data
No: the theorem says good parameters exist, not that training finds them
No: the theorem applies only to polynomial activation functions
5.1-c2.feedback: The theorem guarantees that a good setting of the parameters exists. It says nothing about whether gradient descent reaches it, how long that takes, or how well the result generalizes.

5.2-c1.q: Under the replicator equation, an action’s payoff equals the current average payoff. What happens to its probability at that moment?
options: It grows
It is momentarily unchanged
It shrinks
5.2-c1.feedback: Its rate of change is \(x_i(\pi_i - \bar\pi) = 0\). It may grow or shrink later, as the other probabilities change the average.

5.2-c2.q: A learner trained by reward finds a behavior that exploits a flaw in how reward is computed, and the behavior earns more reward than average. Nobody designed it. What does the selection view predict?
options: It dies out, because nobody intended it
It stays at the same frequency
It becomes more common
5.2-c2.feedback: Selection responds only to reward. A behavior that earns more than average grows, whether or not anyone intended it.

5.3-c1.q: The same random-feature model is fitted to 1,000 noisy training points. Near what number of features would you expect the test error to peak?
options: About 40
About 1,000
About 10,000
5.3-c1.feedback: The peak sits at the interpolation threshold, where the number of features first matches the number of points the model must fit exactly: about 1,000.

5.3-c2.q: Why does ridge regularization remove the peak?
options: It adds features
It removes the noise from the labels
It stops the fit from passing exactly through every noisy point at the threshold
5.3-c2.feedback: The peak comes from a model forced through noisy points with large parameters. The penalty on the parameters lets the fit miss the points a little instead.

5.4-c1.q: Just before test accuracy jumps, is the network only memorizing its training pairs?
options: Yes: the generalizing algorithm appears all at once at the jump
No: the generalizing algorithm is already partly built, but the memorized answers still decide the output
No: by then it has stopped fitting the training pairs
5.4-c1.feedback: In the run on this page, at step 3,600 the full model answers 19% of the test pairs, but its embedding already concentrates on a few frequencies, and the key-frequency part of its output alone would answer 78% of them. The algorithm is partly built; the memorized answers still dominate what the model outputs.

5.4-c2.q: Two copies of this model each answer every training pair correctly. Does that fact alone tell you whether either has learned to add modulo \(p\)?
options: Yes: answering every training pair correctly requires the rule
No: a table of memorized answers and the addition algorithm both get every training pair right
Yes, if both were trained with weight decay
5.4-c2.feedback: Accuracy on the training pairs cannot tell the two solutions apart. Accuracy on pairs the model has not seen, or a look inside the model, can.

5.5-c1.q: Two teams train the same modular-addition transformer on the same data from different seeds, and both reach 100% test accuracy. Team A finds the key frequencies of its model. Can Team B take those to be the key frequencies of its own model?
options: Yes: same architecture, data, and accuracy mean the same algorithm
No: Team B has to examine its own model’s parameters
Yes: the frequencies are fixed by the modulus
5.5-c1.feedback: The five runs in the panel above have the same architecture, data, and test accuracy, and no two use the same set of key frequencies. The modulus does not fix them either: all five compute addition modulo 59. Team B has to examine its own model.

5.5-c2.q: Where would you look to find the rule a trained network uses for a task?
options: In the training code
In the loss function
In its trained parameters and activations, by experiment
5.5-c2.feedback: The training code and the loss say what training rewards, not which mechanism it found. The rule exists only in the trained parameters, and finding it takes investigation of the kind Section 6 describes.

5.6-c1.q: A model gets each digit right with probability 0.9, independently. What is its exact-match accuracy on 10-digit answers?
options: About 0.35
About 0.09
5.6-c1.feedback: \(0.9^{10} \approx 0.35\). A model that is right on 90% of digits is right on only about a third of whole answers.

5.6-c2.q: A benchmark’s exact-match accuracy jumps from 4% to 37% between two model sizes. What would best show whether the underlying ability improved suddenly?
options: A larger benchmark scored the same way
Per-digit accuracy or log-likelihood of the answers for the same models
Testing an even larger model
5.6-c2.feedback: A continuous measure of the same models shows whether the improvement underneath the jump is smooth or sudden.

6.1-c1.q: A probe reads “the input is in French” from layer 6 with 99% accuracy. Does the model use that information?
options: Yes: 99% accuracy shows the model relies on it
The probe does not show it; that needs a causal test
No: if the model used it, a probe would not be needed
6.1-c1.feedback: The probe shows that the information is present at layer 6. Whether the model uses it is a causal question: change the activations along the probed direction, or patch them in from another input, and see whether the model’s behavior changes.

6.1-c2.q: Which result would show that a model uses information about the language of its input?
options: A probe on layer 6 predicts the language with 99% accuracy
A unit of a sparse autoencoder (page 6.5) trained on layer 6 is active on French text and silent on English text
Copying layer 6’s activations from a French input into a run on an English input makes the model answer in French
6.1-c2.feedback: The first two are observations: they show the information is present. The third changes the activations and finds that the output changes, which is causal evidence that the model uses what layer 6 carries.

6.2-c1.q: A direction computed from city statements sorts 99% of the Spanish-word statements correctly. What does this support?
options: That the model has one direction for the truth of every statement
That some single direction separates true from false in both topics
That the model uses this direction when it answers questions
6.2-c1.feedback: The result shows that one direction separates the statements of both topics. Two topics are not every topic, and the differences of means from the three topics point in quite different directions (46° to 66° apart), so there is no evidence here of a single truth direction. Sorting statements also says nothing about whether the model uses the direction. Testing use requires changing the activations and watching the output.

6.3-c1.q: A probe scores 95% on the real task and 93% on its control task. What does that suggest?
options: The model represents the property clearly
The probe is mostly learning the task by itself, so its 95% says little about the model
The model uses the property to produce its outputs
6.3-c1.feedback: The probe nearly fits random labels that carry no information about the property, so its accuracy reflects what it can memorize. Selectivity is 2 points: weak evidence that the representation encodes the property in a readable form.

6.3-c2.q: A linear probe reads a property at 97% with high selectivity. What further test would show that the model uses the property?
options: Train a two-layer probe and compare
Test the probe on more examples of the same kind
Remove or change the probe’s direction in the activations and watch the model’s outputs
6.3-c2.feedback: Accuracy and selectivity are both facts about what can be read out. Use is a causal claim, so it needs an intervention on the activations and a change in behavior.

6.4-c1.q: A toy model stores five features in two dimensions when \(S = 0.9\), but only two when \(S = 0\). Why does sparsity make the difference?
options: Sparse features have smaller values, so they take up less room
Overlapping directions interfere only when several features are active at once, which sparse features rarely are
With sparse features the hidden layer gains extra dimensions
6.4-c1.feedback: The directions overlap at every sparsity once more features than dimensions are stored. The cost of the overlap is paid only on inputs where two or more features are active together. With sparse features such inputs are rare, so the gain from storing more features outweighs the interference.

6.4-c2.q: In a trained model with six features stored in two dimensions, could some rotation of the hidden space make each coordinate respond to exactly one feature?
options: Yes, if the right rotation is found
Yes, but only for the two most important features
No: six directions in a plane cannot each line up with one of only two coordinates
6.4-c2.feedback: A coordinate responds to every feature whose direction has a component along it. Two coordinates can line up with at most two directions; the other four stored features project onto at least one coordinate. Polysemanticity follows from storing more features than dimensions.

6.5-c1.q: An SAE for a layer with 512 neurons is given exactly 512 units. Even with a well-chosen penalty, why might it fail to find the layer’s features?
options: Under superposition the layer can hold more than 512 features, so 512 units are too few
With 512 units the codes cannot be sparse
It will not fail: any 512-dimensional activation is a combination of 512 directions
6.5-c1.feedback: Rebuilding the activations is not the same as recovering the features. Any basis of 512 directions can rebuild a 512-dimensional activation, as the small penalties did in task 1, but under superposition there are more features than dimensions, and each unit can match only one of them.

6.5-c2.q: An SAE rebuilds the activations with almost no error. What does that show about whether its units match the model’s features?
options: They match, since the rebuild is almost perfect
Not much: in the toy, the units matched the features best at a penalty that left a rebuild error of 0.17
They cannot match, since a perfect rebuild needs dense codes
6.5-c2.feedback: With little penalty the SAE rebuilt the toy’s activations almost perfectly while its directions missed most features. Recovery needed a penalty large enough to force sparse codes, at some cost in rebuild error.

6.6-c1.q: A probe finds a “truth” direction at layer 10 with high accuracy. Adding that direction at layer 10, at several coefficients, does not change the model’s outputs. What can you conclude?
options: The probe was wrong: the model does not represent truth
The model represents truth and uses it; steering just failed
Some evidence that the model does not use that direction at that layer for its outputs, unless the intervention was wrong in size or place
6.6-c1.feedback: A probe shows that the information can be read from the direction, never that the model uses it. Steering is the test of use, and a null result counts against use at that layer, with the usual caveat: the coefficient may have been too small, or the model may use the information at another layer or in another form. The tool shows both effects: the same vector does little at some layers and much at others.

6.6-c2.q: Adding a vector at coefficient +10 makes 9 of 10 continuations score as positive, but the text is broken. Has the vector made the model more positive?
options: Yes: the score is what counts
Not clearly: the score must be read together with fluency, since broken text can fool the classifier
No: a steering vector cannot change sentiment
6.6-c2.feedback: A behavior score measured by another model is a proxy. Once the text falls apart, the classifier is scoring fragments, and its output stops tracking what it tracks on fluent text. A steering result is convincing in the range where behavior changes and fluency holds.

6.7-c1.q: For clean 12 + 30 and corrupted 20 + 30, patching head 3 from the clean run into the corrupted run restores about 0% of the logit difference. What does that show?
options: That head 3 plays no part in how the model adds
That head 3 computes nothing about \(a\)
Only that head 3’s clean output is not enough, by itself, to bring back 42 over 50 for this pair
6.7-c1.feedback: Copying from clean to corrupted tests whether an activation is enough to restore the clean answer, for the inputs chosen. Whether head 3 is needed is a different test: replacing head 3’s output with its average over all pairs lowers test accuracy to 49%, more than ablating any other head.

6.7-c2.q: For one clean input and one corrupted input, patching head 3 restores 80% of the logit difference. What should you do before calling head 3 the head that matters?
options: Nothing: 80% settles it
Repeat with many clean and corrupted inputs, and patch the other components too
Patch the MLP instead, since patching heads gives unreliable numbers
6.7-c2.feedback: One pair of inputs can make any head look important. In this model, which head restores the most changes from one pair of inputs to the next, and every head restores 80% or more for some pairs. The numbers are reliable; they answer a question about the inputs chosen.

7.1-c1.q: Two interpreters watch the same coding agent in every situation it could face. One attributes the pair \((P, D)\); the other attributes the pair obtained from it with \(a = 1\), \(b = 0\), \(c = 0.5\), and \(d\) set so that the credences add up to 1. Which attribution does the behavioral evidence favor?
options: The first
The second
Neither: both predict every choice the agent makes
7.1-c1.feedback: The two pairs are related by Bolker’s transformation, so they rank every proposition, and so every action, the same way. No observation of the agent’s choices can tell them apart.

7.1-c2.q: In the Jeffrey-Bolker theory, suppose a probe has been shown to read an agent’s credences exactly. What can two attributions that fit both the behavior and the probe still disagree about?
options: Nothing
The scale and the zero point of the desire function
Which action the agent prefers
7.1-c2.feedback: Fixing \(P\) forces \(c = 0\) and \(d = 1\), which leaves \(D' = aD + b\) with \(a > 0\). The order of the desirabilities is fixed; their unit and zero are not.

7.2-c1.q: A probe has learned to track what most English speakers believe, rather than what is true. On the statements used so far the two always agree. Which criterion can expose the difference, and how?
options: Truth: test the probe on settled questions where common belief is wrong, such as well-known misconceptions
Coherence: test the probe on negations of the training statements
Uniformity: test the probe on another topic
7.2-c1.feedback: Common belief is coherent: most people who believe \(A\) disbelieve not-\(A\), on every topic. So negations and new topics need not separate the two properties. Only statements where the two come apart, true claims most people reject and false claims most people accept, can show that the probe tracks belief rather than truth.

7.3-c1.q: An interpreter removes a set of directions from an agent’s activations, and the agent stops reaching its goal. A second interpreter says those directions carry only the agent’s sense of where the walls are. Which test would tell the two interpretations apart?
options: Remove more directions and see whether the agent fails more often
Swap in, along the same directions, the activations for a different goal, and see whether the agent goes there
Count how often the agent reaches its goal without any intervention
7.3-c1.feedback: Removal shows only that the directions are needed, which is true on both interpretations. If swapping in another goal’s activations along those directions sends the agent to the new goal by a sensible route, the directions carry which goal the agent pursues.

7.3-c2.q: A coding agent has been attributed the desire to finish a task. Halfway through, it starts writing a poem, though nothing in its instructions or in the information available to it has changed. Which criterion does this count against?
options: Intelligibility
Coherence
Use
7.3-c2.feedback: Use requires that a desire steer behavior and that its ends stay stable. A switch of ends with no change in belief to explain it is evidence against a stable desire to finish the task.

7.3-c3.q: After the door intervention, the agent walks to a closed door and stays in front of it, and never reaches its goal. Does this count against attributing the goal to it?
options: Yes, because it no longer reaches the goal
No, because with that belief, going to that door is how to pursue the goal
No, because the network has no beliefs
7.3-c3.feedback: Desire is tested together with belief. An agent that wants the goal and believes the upper door is open should go to the upper door, so the failure is what the attribution predicts for the changed belief.

8.1-c1.q: You pick the best of a million candidate answers using a reward model whose errors are heavy-tailed. What should you expect of the winner?
options: Its true quality is far above average, because a million candidates is strong selection
It probably won because of a large error, and its true quality may be close to average
Its true quality is probably far below average
8.1-c1.feedback: With heavy-tailed errors, the highest proxy scores come mostly from large errors. Independent errors do not push the true value below average; they make the winner’s true value close to that of a typical candidate.

8.1-c2.q: A reward model was trained on answers of ordinary length. During reinforcement learning the policy finds that ever longer answers get ever higher reward, while their true quality drops. Which mechanism is this mainly?
options: Regressional: selection picks up the reward model’s random errors
Extremal: optimization reaches answers far outside the range the reward model was trained on
8.1-c2.feedback: The reward model’s link between length and quality held over ordinary answers. The optimizer pushed into lengths where that link was never checked, as the optimizer in the second panel pushed past the end of the data.

8.2-c1.q: A company scores its support chatbot by the share of users who click “satisfied” after a conversation, and trains the chatbot hard on that score. Which behavior should the company most expect?
options: Telling users what they want to hear, even when it is wrong
Refusing to answer hard questions
Giving correct answers that users dislike
8.2-c1.feedback: The score measures how users feel about an answer, which is easiest to raise by agreeing with them. That is the gap sycophancy exploits: human raters tend to prefer agreeable answers, so a model trained on their ratings learns to agree.

8.2-c2.q: A game agent rewarded for points finds a glitch that lets it collect the same coin again and again. Which of the robot’s exploits is most like this?
options: Tipping the bin to make messes to clean
Blocking the camera
Dragging messes out of view
8.2-c2.feedback: Both create the rewarded event over and over. Blocking the camera and dragging messes away instead change what the measurement sees.

8.3-c1.q: During training with the coin always at the right end, could you have told from the agent’s reward which goal it had learned?
options: Yes: an agent that wanted the right end would have earned less reward
No: both goals earned the same reward on every training level
Yes: its reward would have kept rising for longer
8.3-c1.feedback: On every training level, going to the coin and going to the right end are the same moves with the same reward, so no measurement of training reward can tell them apart. Only a level where the two goals come apart can.

8.3-c2.q: An assistant is trained only on questions whose correct answer is also the answer its users hope for. Which test would show whether it learned “give the correct answer” or “give the answer the user hopes for”?
options: Questions where the correct answer is not the one the user hopes for
More questions like the training questions
Its average reward at the end of training
8.3-c2.feedback: Only cases where the two goals disagree can separate them, like test levels with the coin away from the right end. On training-like questions the two goals give the same answers.

8.4-c1.q: Does the power-seeking theorem of Turner et al. (2021) say that a trained neural network will seek power?
options: Yes, once the network is large enough
No: it concerns optimal policies for randomly drawn rewards; trained networks need not be optimal, and their goals are not random
Yes, for most training runs
8.4-c1.feedback: The 2021 theorem is about optimal policies and distributions over reward functions. Turner and Tadepalli (2022) widen the class of decision procedures, but a trained system still need not satisfy their assumptions, and its goals are not drawn at random.

8.4-c2.q: From the start, one move leads to a single state the agent can never leave, and another leads into a region with 20 such states, any of which it can reach. The agent cannot stay at the start or return to it. Rewards are drawn independently and uniformly for every state, and the discount factor is near 1. Roughly what share of reward functions make the move into the region optimal?
options: About half
About 95%
All of them
8.4-c2.feedback: An agent that cares about the long run goes to the best state it can stay in forever. That state is in the region for 20 of the 21 equally likely cases, about 95%.

8.5-c1.q: In the toy, with detection probability 1 and no honeypots, why does training for 1,000 rounds instead of 100 leave the deceptive share unchanged?
options: Deceptive policies earn the same training reward as aligned ones, so selection cannot tell them apart
Selection is too slow to reach them in 1,000 rounds
Deceptive policies earn more reward than aligned ones
8.5-c1.feedback: The replicator equation changes shares only through differences in reward. A deceptive policy that always recognizes training earns reward 1 on every training input, exactly like an aligned one, so their ratio stays fixed however long training runs.

8.6-c1.q: A lab estimates that its protocol is safe against a red team that tries its best to slip sabotage past the monitor. What does that safety claim not depend on?
options: Whether the model is aligned
Whether the monitor scores sabotage higher than normal work
The size of the audit budget
8.6-c1.feedback: A control argument assumes the worst about the model: it may be misaligned and actively trying to get around oversight. Its safety rests on the monitor, the audits, and the hand-offs, which the lab controls, and on the red team attacking as well as the model could. It does not rest on the model’s goals. Training with human feedback, by contrast, assumes that the model is trying to do what the feedback rewards and that humans can judge the outputs.

9.1-c1.q: A reader has finished pages 6.3 and 7.2 and nothing in Section 4. Using the filter, which problem are they best prepared for?
options: Probes that generalize
Reward model overoptimization
Is written reasoning faithful?
9.1-c1.feedback: “Probes that generalize” builds on 6.3 (linear probes) and 7.2 (belief). Reward model overoptimization needs 4.3, and the question about written reasoning needs 4.4.
